opening.text: Think of the best gift you ever received. Maybe it was a bicycle, a book, or a coat on a cold day. Did you pay for it? Probably not. Someone gave it to you because they loved you. You could say thank you. You could use it well. But you could not buy it, because then it would no longer be a gift.
Grace is like that. It is a gift from God, and it comes through Jesus Christ.
I would like to talk about grace.

mainMessage.text: Grace is the help and mercy God gives us through His Son. It is a gift. We cannot earn it. But we do not receive it passively either. We come to Christ, we repent, we try, and His grace makes up what we lack. It forgives us. It changes us. It strengthens us when we are weak. Grace is how we get home.

blocks.text: Grace is a gift, and it is for everyone.
Paul told the Ephesians that we are saved by grace, through faith, and that it is a gift of God. He also taught Titus that the grace of God has appeared to all people. No one is left out.
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.
For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “All Men Everywhere” from the April 2006 general conference.

These teachings that the resurrecting and cleansing power of the Atonement is for all contradict the assertion that the grace of God saves only a chosen few. His grace is for all. These teachings of the Book of Mormon expand our vision and enlarge our understanding of the all-encompassing love of God and the universal effect of His Atonement for all men everywhere.
His grace is for all. That includes you.
We cannot earn it.

We should do good works. But no amount of good work can pay for what the Savior did. King Benjamin said that even if we served God with our whole souls, we would still be unprofitable servants. We owe Him everything. And Lehi taught his son Jacob that no one can live in God’s presence except through the merits, mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah.

I say unto you that if ye should serve him who has created you from the beginning, and is preserving you from day to day, by lending you breath, that ye may live and move and do according to your own will, and even supporting you from one moment to another—I say, if ye should serve him with all your whole souls yet ye would be unprofitable servants.

Wherefore, how great the importance to make these things known unto the inhabitants of the earth, that they may know that there is no flesh that can dwell in the presence of God, save it be through the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah, who layeth down his life according to the flesh, and taketh it again by the power of the Spirit, that he may bring to pass the resurrection of the dead, being the first that should rise.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote this in his article “Another Testament of Jesus Christ” in the March 1994 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.

After all our obedience and good works, we cannot be saved from death or the effects of our individual sins without the grace extended by the atonement of Jesus Christ. The Book of Mormon makes this clear. It teaches that ‘salvation doth not come by the law alone’ (Mosiah 13:28). In other words, salvation does not come simply by keeping the commandments. . . . Even those who try to obey and serve God with all their heart, might, mind, and strength are ‘unprofitable servants’ (Mosiah 2:21). Man cannot earn his own salvation.
That is not bad news. It is the reason we need Him, and the reason we can have hope.
Grace covers what we cannot fix.

Every one of us makes mistakes. Some are small. Some are heavy. We cannot undo them on our own. But Nephi taught that we are saved by grace, after all we can do. We do our part. We come to Christ and we try. And His grace does what we cannot.

For we labor diligently to write, to persuade our children, and also our brethren, to believe in Christ, and to be reconciled to God; for we know that it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.

Yea, come unto Christ, and be perfected in him, and deny yourselves of all ungodliness; and if ye shall deny yourselves of all ungodliness, and love God with all your might, mind and strength, then is his grace sufficient for you, that by his grace ye may be perfect in Christ; and if by the grace of God ye are perfect in Christ, ye can in nowise deny the power of God.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote this in his article “Moral Agency” in the June 2009 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.

Just as death would doom us and render our agency meaningless but for the redemption of Christ, even so, without His grace, our sins and bad choices would leave us forever lost. There would be no way of fully recovering from our mistakes, and being unclean, we could never live again in the presence of \[God\].
Without grace, we would be lost. With it, we can come home.
Grace changes us.

Grace does not only forgive. It also changes us. King Benjamin’s people said the Spirit had wrought a mighty change in their hearts. They had no more desire to do evil, but to do good continually. Alma asked the people of his day if they had felt that same change.

And they all cried with one voice, saying: Yea, we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us; and also, we know of their surety and truth, because of the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, which has wrought a mighty change in us, or in our hearts, that we have no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually.
And now behold, I ask of you, my brethren of the church, have ye spiritually been born of God? Have ye received his image in your countenances? Have ye experienced this mighty change in your hearts?
Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Ye Must Be Born Again” from the April 2007 general conference.

The essence of the gospel of Jesus Christ entails a fundamental and permanent change in our very nature made possible through our reliance upon ‘the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah’ (2 Nephi 2:8). As we choose to follow the Master, we choose to be changed—to be spiritually reborn.
Grace does not leave us the same. It makes us new.
Grace gives us strength in our weakness.

The Lord told Moroni that He gives men weakness so they may be humble. And if they come to Him in faith, He will make weak things strong. Paul heard the same thing. When he asked the Lord for relief, the Lord answered that His grace was enough.

And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness that they may be humble; and my grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me; for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

David A. Bednar, then president of Brigham Young University–Idaho and now a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, said this in his Brigham Young University devotional address “In the Strength of the Lord” on October 23, 2001. It is a devotional, not a conference talk.

. . . It is especially interesting to me that Nephi did not pray . . . to have his circumstances changed. Rather, he prayed for the strength to change his circumstances. And may I suggest that he prayed in this manner precisely because he knew and understood and had experienced the enabling power of the Atonement of the Savior.
Grace is not only a way out of trouble. It is strength to walk through it.
Grace lightens our load, and lifts us a step at a time.

The Lord invites all who are weary to come to Him. He offers rest. He also showed, in His own life, that growth comes one step at a time. John said He went from grace to grace until He received a fulness. We can follow that pattern too.

And I, John, saw that he received not of the fulness at the first, but received grace for grace; And he received not of the fulness at first, but continued from grace to grace, until he received a fulness;

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
Elder Donald L. Hallstrom of the Seventy said this in his talk “Turn to the Lord” from the April 2010 general conference.

. . . And, without delay, turn to the Lord. Exercise all of the faith you have in Him. Let Him share your burden. Allow His grace to lighten your load. . . . Never let an earthly circumstance disable you spiritually.
We do not have to carry it all. We can let Him help.

story.title: The prodigal son

blocks.text: A young man had left home and wasted what he had been given. When he finally decided to go back, he planned to ask to be a servant. But he never got to finish his speech.

And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. And the son said unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son. But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet: And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry: For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.
The son did nothing to earn the robe, the ring, or the feast. He only came home. The father saw him from far away and ran. That is what grace looks like. God runs to meet us when we turn toward Him.

opening.text: Imagine standing at the edge of a deep canyon. On the other side is where you want to be. You look for a way across. You cannot jump it. You cannot climb down and up. You may spend years looking for a path. But then someone shows you a bridge that was already built for you.

mainMessage.text: Grace is the divine help that comes to us through Jesus Christ. It is a gift. We cannot earn our way back to God. But we are asked to walk across the bridge. A bridge does nothing if you will not step onto it. Nephi said that we are saved by grace, after all we can do. We do what we can. We come to Christ. We love God and deny ourselves of what pulls us away. And His grace is enough for what remains.

story.title: The woman brought to Jesus

blocks.text: A group of men brought a woman to Jesus. They wanted to trap Him. They said the law of Moses called for her to be stoned. Jesus answered them.

So when they continued asking him, he lifted up himself, and said unto them, He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her. And again he stooped down, and wrote on the ground. And they which heard it, being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last: and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst. When Jesus had lifted up himself, and saw none but the woman, he said unto her, Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee? She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.

The Savior did not excuse sin. He said, “go, and sin no more.” But He did not condemn her either. He gave her a way forward. That is grace. It meets us where we are, and it points us to a better path.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time about grace. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The thief on the cross

blocks.text: Two criminals were crucified beside Jesus. One mocked Him. The other spoke up.

And one of the malefactors which were hanged railed on him, saying, If thou be Christ, save thyself and us. But the other answering rebuked him, saying, Dost not thou fear God, seeing thou art in the same condemnation? And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss. And he said unto Jesus, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.

This man had no time to repay a debt. He did not have a long record of good works to show. What he had was honesty. He said what was true, and he turned to the Savior. And the Savior answered him with mercy. We do not know the rest of his story. But we know that the Lord did not turn away.

application.text: First, think of a debt you carry that only the Savior can pay, such as a mistake you cannot undo. Take it to Him in prayer. Second, show gratitude to Him this week with one act of service, done in His name. Third, if someone owes you something, such as an apology or a favor, offer them the grace you hope to receive.

closingVerse.text: And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people. And he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which bind his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.

opening.text: Picture a person at the bottom of a deep pit. The walls are smooth. They try to climb out, and they slip. They shout, and no one hears. Then a ladder comes down from above. Someone is holding the top. The person in the pit still has to climb. But now there is a way.
That is a picture of grace. I would like to talk about it today.

mainMessage.text: Grace is God’s help, given to us through Jesus Christ. We are not able to get out of the pit by ourselves. Jesus lowers the ladder. We climb, and He holds it steady. His grace forgives us, changes us, and strengthens us. It is a gift, and it is offered to every one of us.

blocks.text: The ladder is lowered for everyone.
Paul wrote that we are saved by grace through faith, and that it is God’s gift. He also wrote that the grace of God has appeared to all. No one is too deep in the pit for the ladder to reach.
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.
For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught this in his talk “All Men Everywhere” from the April 2006 general conference.

These teachings that the resurrecting and cleansing power of the Atonement is for all contradict the assertion that the grace of God saves only a chosen few. His grace is for all. These teachings of the Book of Mormon expand our vision and enlarge our understanding of the all-encompassing love of God and the universal effect of His Atonement for all men everywhere.
His grace is for all. It reaches every pit.
We cannot climb out alone.

Smooth walls do not give a handhold. We cannot lift ourselves out by our own effort. King Benjamin said that if we served God with all our souls, we would still be unprofitable servants. And Lehi taught Jacob that no one can dwell in God’s presence without the merits, mercy, and grace of the Messiah.

I say unto you that if ye should serve him who has created you from the beginning, and is preserving you from day to day, by lending you breath, that ye may live and move and do according to your own will, and even supporting you from one moment to another—I say, if ye should serve him with all your whole souls yet ye would be unprofitable servants.

Wherefore, how great the importance to make these things known unto the inhabitants of the earth, that they may know that there is no flesh that can dwell in the presence of God, save it be through the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah, who layeth down his life according to the flesh, and taketh it again by the power of the Spirit, that he may bring to pass the resurrection of the dead, being the first that should rise.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught this in his article “Another Testament of Jesus Christ” in the March 1994 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.

After all our obedience and good works, we cannot be saved from death or the effects of our individual sins without the grace extended by the atonement of Jesus Christ. The Book of Mormon makes this clear. It teaches that ‘salvation doth not come by the law alone’ (Mosiah 13:28). In other words, salvation does not come simply by keeping the commandments. . . . Even those who try to obey and serve God with all their heart, might, mind, and strength are ‘unprofitable servants’ (Mosiah 2:21). Man cannot earn his own salvation.
We need the ladder. That is the honest truth.
We climb, and He holds the ladder.

The person in the pit has to take hold and climb. Nephi taught that we are saved by grace, after all we can do. We come to Christ. We turn away from what pulls us down. And His grace is sufficient. It holds the ladder steady.

For we labor diligently to write, to persuade our children, and also our brethren, to believe in Christ, and to be reconciled to God; for we know that it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.

Yea, come unto Christ, and be perfected in him, and deny yourselves of all ungodliness; and if ye shall deny yourselves of all ungodliness, and love God with all your might, mind and strength, then is his grace sufficient for you, that by his grace ye may be perfect in Christ; and if by the grace of God ye are perfect in Christ, ye can in nowise deny the power of God.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught this in his article “Moral Agency” in the June 2009 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.

Just as death would doom us and render our agency meaningless but for the redemption of Christ, even so, without His grace, our sins and bad choices would leave us forever lost. There would be no way of fully recovering from our mistakes, and being unclean, we could never live again in the presence of \[God\].
We do our part. He makes it possible.
We come out different.

A person who has climbed out of a pit does not return to it. King Benjamin’s people said the Spirit had wrought a mighty change in their hearts. They had no more desire to do evil, but to do good continually. Alma asked us if we have felt this change.

And they all cried with one voice, saying: Yea, we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us; and also, we know of their surety and truth, because of the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, which has wrought a mighty change in us, or in our hearts, that we have no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually.
And now behold, I ask of you, my brethren of the church, have ye spiritually been born of God? Have ye received his image in your countenances? Have ye experienced this mighty change in your hearts?
Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught this in his talk “Ye Must Be Born Again” from the April 2007 general conference.

The essence of the gospel of Jesus Christ entails a fundamental and permanent change in our very nature made possible through our reliance upon ‘the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah’ (2 Nephi 2:8). As we choose to follow the Master, we choose to be changed—to be spiritually reborn.
Grace does not only lift us out. It makes us new.
He gives us strength for each rung.

Some rungs are hard to reach. We may feel too tired or too weak. The Lord told Moroni that if we humble ourselves and have faith, He will make weak things strong. He told Paul that His grace is enough. The strength is His to give.

And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness that they may be humble; and my grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me; for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

David A. Bednar, then president of Brigham Young University–Idaho and now a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, taught this in his Brigham Young University devotional address “In the Strength of the Lord” on October 23, 2001. It is a devotional, not a conference talk.

. . . It is especially interesting to me that Nephi did not pray . . . to have his circumstances changed. Rather, he prayed for the strength to change his circumstances. And may I suggest that he prayed in this manner precisely because he knew and understood and had experienced the enabling power of the Atonement of the Savior.
Pray for strength to climb. He will give it.
We can put down what is too heavy.

Some people climb out of the pit carrying a heavy pack. The Savior invites us to put it down. He says His yoke is easy and His burden is light. He also shows us that growth is gradual. Even He went from grace to grace.

And I, John, saw that he received not of the fulness at the first, but received grace for grace; And he received not of the fulness at first, but continued from grace to grace, until he received a fulness;

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
Elder Donald L. Hallstrom of the Seventy taught this in his talk “Turn to the Lord” from the April 2010 general conference.

. . . And, without delay, turn to the Lord. Exercise all of the faith you have in Him. Let Him share your burden. Allow His grace to lighten your load. . . . Never let an earthly circumstance disable you spiritually.
We can put the burden down. He will carry it with us.

story.title: Alma’s cry for mercy

blocks.text: Alma the Younger had once worked against the church. Later, he was filled with pain over what he had done. He told his son Helaman what happened in his darkest hour.

And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my many sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world. Now, as my mind caught hold upon this thought, I cried within my heart: O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me, who am in the gall of bitterness, and am encircled about by the everlasting chains of death. And now, behold, when I thought this, I could remember my pains no more; yea, I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins no more. And oh, what joy, and what marvelous light I did behold; yea, my soul was filled with joy as exceeding as was my pain!

Alma could not climb out of that pit by himself. But his mind “caught hold” of the Savior. He asked for mercy. And the ladder came down. The pain turned into joy. When we reach for Jesus, grace reaches back.

application.text: First, name the pit you feel stuck in. Then say Alma’s short prayer in your own words: “Jesus, have mercy on me.” Second, take one small step this week to climb, such as repenting of one habit or reaching out to a bishop. Third, hold the ladder for someone else. Encourage a person who feels stuck.

As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.

Grace is like that hand. It does not pedal for us. But it steadies us, again and again, until we can go further than we thought we could.
I would like to talk about the grace of Jesus Christ.

story.title: Jesus restores Peter

blocks.text: Peter had said he would never leave the Lord. Then, on the night of the arrest, he denied knowing Him three times. After the Resurrection, Jesus met Peter by the sea.

So when they had dined, Jesus saith to Simon Peter, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my lambs. He saith to him again the second time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my sheep. He saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me? And he said unto him, Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. Jesus saith unto him, Feed my sheep.

Three times Peter had denied Him. Three times the Savior asked about his love, and three times gave him work to do. He did not shame Peter. He trusted him again. That is grace. It gives us another chance, and a purpose.

application.text: First, think of a place where you keep wobbling. Ask the Lord for strength, and take one small step. Second, give someone else a second chance this week. Third, ask yourself the Savior’s question: “Lovest thou me?” Then think of one way to show it by feeding someone, in the way they need.
